newsitem.title: USA: Kentucky, Indiana awash in cresting Ohio River.
newsitem.headline: Kentucky, Indiana awash in cresting Ohio River.

text.p: Authorities offered free tetanus shots and ordered hundreds of thousands of Kentuckians to boil their drinking water on Friday as dirty floodwaters from the rising Ohio River crept higher.

The swollen river was expected to crest on Friday evening at 16 feet (5 metres) above its normal flood stage at Louisville. The city was protected by massive flood walls that should hold back the river's highest crest since 1964.

Upstream and downstream from Louisville, homes that formerly sat on the edge of the Ohio River were inundated by the expanding waterway. National Guard troops and prison inmates joined townspeople in constructing sandbag barriers and pumping out the relentless floodwaters.

Nearly 200,000 residents in Kentucky were told to boil tap water before drinking it after floodwaters submerged at least 40 residential water systems. Tetanus and diptheria shots were offered free to those who have not been inoculated recently in flood-ravaged areas in Kentucky and in Cincinnati, Ohio.
"The floodwaters were muddy at the very least, and possibly contaminated with other substances," said Mike Lynch of the Kentucky Disaster and Emergency Services.

The body of a man was pulled from the Ohio River in the Louisville area on Friday and a woman missing since Saturday was found in southern Kentucky when local floodwaters receded, raising Kentucky's death toll to 18. In West Virginia, authorities found a car with the bodies of two women nurses who attempted to steer around a barricade blocking a flooded road, lifting the state's fatality count to three.
A total of 59 deaths have been blamed on last Saturday's tornadoes in Arkansas and flooding from the same storm system that followed.
Forecasts for rain or snow this weekend in hard-hit western Kentucky and Tennessee may worsen an already bad situation, and slow the siphoning off of the floodwaters, officials said.

Psychologists from surrounding states offered their services free of charge at Red Cross shelters, and warned flood victims to be aware of signs of lingering stress such as recurring nightmares, edginess, depression and memory gaps.
Downstream from Louisville at West Point, Kentucky, two dozen stubborn residents stayed behind as swirling waters from the Ohio River engulfed the town.

"Some people just don't want to come out," said Mililani Chun, spokesperson for the Hardin County Disaster and Emergency Services. "Yesterday we were in a speedboat and we ran across a man who was fishing from his backyard."

Eddie Moore of the Westpoint Fire Department said an elderly woman he offered to rescue from her marooned home refused. "She said she has lived through two floods before and she is going to live through this one," he said.

The Ohio was receding fairly rapidly in Cincinnati, but was not expected to crest downstream in Evansville, Indiana, until Tuesday. The river then feeds into the Mississippi River, which widens out and should not pose a flood danger.
